newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan stocks seen rosier if stability restored.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan stocks seen rosier if stability restored.

text.p: Pakistani stocks are likely to rebound after elections set for February 3, but analysts said it was not clear if the rise could be sustained.
They said political instability and economic troubles might continue to hound the depressed Karachi market, which is struggling to attract fresh investment despite cheap valuations.
Political chaos descended when President Farooq Leghari sacked Benazir Bhutto's government on November 5 on disputed charges of corruption and misrule.
He appointed a caretaker government led by Prime Minister Meraj Khalid to supervise national and provincial polls, launch a drive against corruption and initiate economic reforms.
The Karachi Stock Exchange 100-share index ended at 1,391.62 on Sunday, a 25 percent decline from its year-high of 1,855.22 points on February 15.

"Unless there is a sustained improvement on the economic and political fronts over the next four to six months, you cannot be very optimistic over a one-year horizon," analyst Nadeem Naqvi of International Asset Management Co Ltd (IAMC), an affiliate of Morgan Stanley Asset Management Inc, told Reuters.
He said fresh funds might flow into the cash-strapped market by the end of the first quarter on the back of an improved political scenario after the February 3 elections.
"But as long as there is economic uncertainty, index growth will remain capped," he said.

The caretaker government has announced several measures to put the troubled economy back on track, but the market has remained unmoved amid uncertainty about whether a new, elected government will implement the policies of its predecessor.
Naqvi said some measures announced by the interim government were not only difficult to implement, but might also make it more difficult to raise new money for equity investment.
"I see more pain before any gain," he said.
Analyst Nauman Sheikh of KASB & Co said the reforms, if implemented successfully, could lay the groundwork for a sustained rise, but said a bull run was unlikely.
"Any sharp rise is likely to be countered by off-loading of old portfolios to book profits or cut losses," Sheikh said.
He said the market could rise to 1,850 just on local support and could reach 2,000 by end-1997, if all went well.

Anisur Rehman, research head at Crosby Securities, said the index could rise to 2,040 points in the next six months, but cautioned that the market had a weak retail base and was too dependent on funds pumped in by foreign and local institutions.

"Any major movements above the 1,900-point level would witness net selling, but we do expect some reallocation of regional portfolios away from Asian markets, which had experienced sharp rises during the past year, towards markets like Pakistan," Naqvi said.
He said Pakistan's current high risk profile had driven foreign investors' expected rate of return to 28-30 percent.
Yet even if the index hit 1,600 points from its present level of around 1,400, the quarterly return would be not more than 14.3 percent, he added.
